title: Implementing a secure underwriting system: a CIO's guide
summary: How CIOs implement a secure underwriting system: controls to require, how to connect it to your policy admin system and a 90-day modular rollout.
body_markdown:
A secure underwriting system is one where every submission, every AI-extracted field and every underwriting decision stays inside controls your security team can name and audit, from the moment a broker email lands to the moment a quote goes out. For a CIO, implementing one comes down to six decisions made in the right order: which data the system will touch, how it connects to your policy admin system, who can see what, how every change is logged, what evidence the vendor hands over, and which stage of underwriting goes live first. We think the last decision matters more than most security reviews admit, because a system rolled out one stage at a time gives your team a narrow, testable data flow to approve, where a big-bang rollout asks them to sign off on everything at once.


## What makes an underwriting system secure in 2026?


Underwriting data is some of the most sensitive data a carrier or MGA holds, and the regulatory weight on it keeps growing, so security for an underwriting system has to start with the data itself before it reaches the vendor questionnaire. A typical commercial submission carries a mix that few other systems in the enterprise see in one place:


- Personal information on owners, drivers and employees, including dates of birth, license numbers and payroll detail.
- Financial statements, tax figures and revenue breakdowns that the insured shares under the assumption of confidentiality.
- Loss runs and claims history, which in workers' compensation and healthcare-adjacent lines can include injury and treatment detail.
- Your own appetite rules, pricing logic and underwriting guidelines, which are competitive assets in their own right.


The rules around that data are getting stricter as well. New York's Department of Financial Services set the tone when,[according to NYDFS](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity) , it issued its first-in-the-nation cybersecurity regulation, 23 NYCRR Part 500, on March 1, 2017, and the[NAIC Insurance Data Security Model Law (#668)](https://content.naic.org/insurance-topics/cybersecurity) asks licensees in adopting states to run an information security program, investigate cybersecurity events and notify the commissioner. AI adds a further layer, since the[NAIC model bulletin on insurers' use of AI](https://content.naic.org/insurance-topics/artificial-intelligence) , adopted in December 2023, states that decisions made or supported by AI must comply with all applicable insurance laws. The cost of getting it wrong is also rising, with[IBM's Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026](https://www.ibm.com/reports/data-breach) putting the global average breach at a record $4.99M, up 12% on the prior year.


## Which security controls should a CIO require before go-live?


We suggest treating the controls below as the minimum a vendor should evidence before any production submission flows through the new system, and our earlier piece on[what carriers must verify before trusting an AI vendor](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/data-security-underwriting-automation-what-carriers-must-verify) goes deeper on the vendor evaluation itself. The point of the table is to pair each control with the evidence that proves it, so that the review rests on documents your team can file rather than answers on a sales call.


Control What to ask for Evidence to file


Independent certification SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001, with a scope that covers the AI extraction and inference services Latest SOC 2 report under NDA, ISO 27001 certificate and its statement of applicability


Identity and access Single sign-on through your identity provider (SAML or OIDC) and role-based permissions SSO configuration record and a role matrix signed off by underwriting leadership


Audit trail and data lineage A log of every action, showing what the AI extracted and what a person changed Sample audit export for one test submission, reviewed by internal audit


Data use and retention Written terms on how your submissions may be used, how long they are kept and how they are deleted Contract clauses and the vendor's retention schedule


Incident response Notice timelines that let you meet your own state and NYDFS obligations Incident response plan summary and named contacts on both sides


AI governance A documented approach to model changes, testing and human review, mapped to a framework such as the[NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework) Model change log and the human-review policy for each workflow


## How should an underwriting system connect to your policy admin system?


The integration pattern decides how many copies of your data exist and how many doors lead to them, so it deserves a security decision of its own before any field mapping starts. Most carriers and MGAs choose between three patterns, and each has a different security footprint:


- Headless, behind your policy admin system. The AI stages run through a REST API and return structured data into the system your underwriters already use, which keeps the user interface and its access controls where they are today.
- Hybrid. Some stages return data by API while others run in the vendor's interface, which suits teams that want new screens for rating or portfolio work while keeping intake inside existing tools.
- Full operating environment. Underwriters work in the vendor's system end to end, with single sign-on and role-based permissions carrying your access rules across.


Whichever pattern you choose, a few habits shrink the attack surface considerably. Connect intake to the submissions inbox you already have rather than asking brokers to send to a new address, use scoped service accounts with least-privilege API keys instead of shared credentials, prefer webhook callbacks over scheduled bulk exports so that data moves only when a submission does, and retire legacy file shares once the API path is live. It is also worth confirming early which stages can run headless at all, since in many systems the stages up to risk analysis can sit behind your policy admin system while rating, quoting and portfolio views need the vendor's own interface. Clean, verified data at intake helps here as well, because, as we covered in[the real cost of inaccurate underwriting data](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/real-cost-inaccurate-underwriting-data-commercial-p-c) , every manual re-key creates another spreadsheet that lives outside your controls.


## Why does a modular rollout lower security risk?


A modular rollout lowers security risk because each stage you switch on brings a single, well-defined data flow that your security team can review and test before the next one arrives. Underwriting breaks naturally into six stages, and each touches a different slice of your data:


Stage Data it touches Security review focus


Intake and clearance Broker emails, attachments, insured names, existing policy records Mailbox access scope, duplicate-check queries against your systems


Extraction and research ACORD forms, loss runs, schedules, public web and registry data Personal data handling, which outside sources are queried


Triage and risk analysis Appetite rules, scoring factors, guidelines Protection of proprietary rules, explainability for regulators


Rating and pricing Rating algorithms, filed rates, pricing authority limits Change control on rating logic, approval workflows


Quote and bind Quote documents, terms, broker communications Outbound document controls, who can issue and bind


Portfolio management Book-level premium, hit ratio and exposure data Reporting access by role, data export rules


Starting with intake and clearance is often the safest first step, since it touches the narrowest set of systems and pays back quickly in capacity, a point we made in our guide to[submission intake best practices](https://www.pibit.ai/blog/submission-intake-best-practices-commercial-pc) . Your team learns the vendor's controls on one data flow, internal audit tests the audit trail on real submissions, and each later stage inherits an identity model and logging setup that have already passed review. A full replacement project, by contrast, tends to bundle every data flow into one approval, which is how exceptions get waved through under deadline pressure.


## What does a 90-day secure implementation plan look like?


A 90-day plan gives security, underwriting and IT a shared timeline in which each phase ends with something your team can test, and we suggest structuring it in four steps:


1. Weeks 1 to 2, classify and decide. Map the data each stage will touch, choose the integration pattern, collect the vendor's SOC 2 report and ISO 27001 certificate under NDA, and agree data use and retention terms in the contract.
2. Weeks 2 to 4, connect identity and logging. Set up single sign-on, build the role matrix with underwriting leadership, and route the vendor's audit events to the tools your security operations team already watches.
3. Weeks 4 to 8, run the first stage live. Switch on one stage, usually[submission intake](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/submission-intake) and[submission clearance](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/submission-clearance) , on a single line of business, and have internal audit sample the audit trail on live submissions.
4. Weeks 8 to 12, review and extend. Hold a joint security and underwriting review, close any findings, and only then add the next stage, such as extraction and research or triage and risk analysis.


The pace is realistic because a modular system does not need a core-system replacement to go live, and the first stage gives your underwriters capacity back while the security work continues on firm ground. If you run delegated programs, it is also worth extending the same audit-trail review to the data that MGAs and coverholders working under your[delegated underwriting authority](https://www.pibit.ai/insurance-knowledge/delegated-underwriting-authority) send in, since that data enters through the same front door.
